findings.heading: Import dataset
findings.proposition: The English carries a level-3 section heading '### Import dataset {.unnumbered}'; in Portuguese the same words appear as an ordinary paragraph line ('Importar conjunto de dados'), so no heading exists and the import content is absorbed into the 'Carregar Pacotes' section.
findings.reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader gets no entry for the data-import step in the table of contents or the section numbering, and cannot navigate or link to it; the import instructions read as a stray sentence inside the package-loading section.

findings.heading: Overview
findings.proposition: The English says the chapter focuses on 'right censoring' (a named censoring type); the Portuguese says it focuses on 'censura correta' ('correct censoring'), which is not a censoring type and is not supported by the English.
findings.reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader does not learn that only right censoring is treated, so they may assume the chapter's methods cover left and interval censoring too, and they cannot connect the text to the standard term 'censura à direita' used in other sources.

findings.heading: Building a surv-type object
findings.proposition: The English says the '+' in the printed Surv object marks an observation that was right-censored; the Portuguese says it marks an observation that was 'bem censurada' ('well censored'), which the English does not support.
findings.reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader misreads the '+' symbol as a quality flag on the censoring rather than as the marker of right-censoring, and so cannot correctly interpret the printed Surv vector.

findings.heading: Plotting Kaplan-Meir curves
findings.proposition: The English states that the proportion of participants surviving BEYOND 60 days of follow-up is around 40%; the Portuguese states that the proportion surviving 'nos ultimos 60 dias de seguimento' ('in the last 60 days of follow-up') is around 40%.
findings.reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader reads the 40% as applying to a trailing 60-day window instead of to survival past day 60, and therefore reads the Kaplan-Meier curve at the wrong point.

findings.heading: Cox regression analysis
findings.proposition: The English says the hazard ratio is analogous to an ODDS RATIO in multiple logistic regression; the Portuguese says it is analogous to a 'taxa de probabilidade' (a probability rate), which is a different quantity from an odds ratio.
findings.reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader is given a false analogy and may interpret the hazard ratio as a ratio of probabilities, losing the link to the odds ratio they already know from logistic regression.

findings.heading: Cox regression analysis
findings.proposition: The English third bullet says that if the HR (hazard ratio) is greater than 1 the predictor is associated with increased risk; the Portuguese third bullet makes the claim about 'a FC', an abbreviation the English does not use and which in Portuguese medical writing denotes heart rate ('frequencia cardiaca').
findings.reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader sees the interpretation rule attached to an undefined or wrong quantity, breaking the three-bullet HR interpretation list and leaving the greater-than-1 case without a stated referent.

findings.heading: Fitting a Cox model
findings.proposition: The English says a continuous predictor's parameter estimate is the increase in the expected LOG of the relative hazard per one-unit increase; the Portuguese says it is the increase in the expected 'registo' (record/register) of the relative hazard, dropping the logarithm.
findings.reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader does not learn that the coefficient is on the log-hazard scale, so they may read coef directly as a hazard ratio and skip the exponentiation needed to interpret it.

findings.heading: Fitting a Cox model
findings.proposition: The English names the comparison group for the 1.21x increased risk of death: patients whose source of infection was OTHER THAN FUNERALS. The Portuguese says only 'pacientes que tem outra fonte de infeccao' without stating what it is other than.
findings.reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader cannot tell which level of 'source' is the reference, so they cannot say whether funeral infection or non-funeral infection carries the higher hazard, and the earlier funeral-survival-benefit statement is left unconnected.

findings.heading: Add unique patient identifier
findings.proposition: The English states that rowid_to_column() comes from the tidyverse package TIBBLE; the Portuguese attributes it only to 'o pacote tidyverse' and names no member package.
findings.reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader who does not load the whole tidyverse cannot tell which package to load or namespace-qualify to reach rowid_to_column(), and the code fails with 'could not find function'.

findings.heading: Expand patient rows
findings.proposition: The English states the goal of the restructuring: create a separate row for each patient for each time interval in which that patient has a different value of deltaA. The Portuguese omits this sentence and jumps straight to the consequence (at most two rows per patient).
findings.reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader is told the row count but not the rule that produces it, so they cannot generalise tmerge() to a covariate with more than two states and do not know that rows are split at changes in the time-dependent covariate.

findings.heading: Time-dependent covariates in survival models
findings.proposition: The English says the previous Cox analyses rely on the COVARIATE being measured at baseline; the Portuguese says they rely on 'a covariancia' (the covariance) being measured at baseline.
findings.reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader is pointed at the wrong object: the stated limitation of standard Cox regression becomes a claim about a covariance rather than about when each predictor is measured, which is the whole motivation for the time-dependent setup that follows.
